Following up on his earlier warning against post-misbehavior reminders, Linsin describes a proactive reminder technique used before misbehavior can occur.

t: Why Reminders Make Classroom Management More Difficult ent-more-difficult/
q: If there is one classroom management mistake made more often than others, it is the practice of giving reminders after misbehavior has already occurred.
Every time you give a reminder in response to misbehavior, you fail to follow through with your classroom management plan.
So naturally when you ask them to line up quietly with their hands at their sides, to them it doesn’t really mean you expect them to do it—at least not the first time you ask.

When your first reaction to misbehavior is to give a reminder, you’re communicating to your students that you don’t really mean what you say—unless, that is, you raise your voice, lose your cool, or otherwise show your frustration.
If you give a lot of reminders, your words won’t pack any punch. Your voice will no more cut through the static in their heads than the soft drone of a Hummingbird outside your classroom window.

If you just make this one change, if you decide that you’re no longer going to give post-misbehavior reminders—and instead follow your classroom management plan as it’s written—you will notice dramatic improvement in behavior.
x: Giving a reminder after misbehavior instead of enforcing a consequence undermines a teacher's classroom management plan.

Linsin identifies reactive reminders — restating expectations after misbehavior has already occurred — as the most common classroom management mistake teachers make.
The transition away from reminders will be difficult at first, with rough early days before students adjust.

t: How To Repair A Broken Relationship With Your Students ur-students/
q: It’s best to wait until the next morning before addressing the incident that precipitated your outburst.
Say simply, “Yesterday I was unhappy with the way you behaved during math, and I handled it poorly. I lost my cool and I’m sorry.
Now is your opportunity to do what you should have done instead of losing your cool. Hold your students accountable for the previous days’ behavior.
Resist the urge to try to win them back with a fun afternoon, a silly game, or an easing of your behavior standards. These methods are manipulative.
Trust is built over time with your consistent behavior. It’s an hour-by-hour, day-by-day sameness that restores rapport and influence.
One of the keys to keeping your cool is to never let behavior reach the point where it gets under your skin.
x: Wait until the next morning to address an outburst, giving both teacher and students a fresh start.
Linsin offers a recovery plan for teachers who lose their cool, raise their voice, or otherwise damage trust with their class.
Still hold students accountable for the behavior that triggered the outburst; apologizing doesn't erase their responsibility.

t: A Simple Way To Build Rapport With Difficult Students students/
q: One of the most effective ways to do this is with a simple note, written in your hand, folded over, and taped to the top or side of their desk.
What you say in your note is less important than its genuineness. For if you don’t truly believe what you say, your students will find you out.
You mustn’t mention the note to the student and it’s best not to watch them while they read it.
An oft-repeated phrase on this website is that there is no magic to your classroom management plan. And it’s true.
A simple note, though, just between the two of you, has a way of cutting through their negative views of school and of teachers.
x: A short, handwritten, genuine note left privately on a student's desk can build rapport more effectively than direct interaction.
The note's content matters less than its genuineness — simple, brief statements of belief in the student, left privately without follow-up commentary.
Teachers should not watch students read the note or make a big deal of it afterward — the moment should remain private.

Linsin recommends a subtle, low-key strategy for connecting with difficult students who are guarded and skeptical after years of failed teacher tactics: a short, handwritten, genuine note left on or near their desk.

t: Dealing With Difficult Students - The First Critical Step al-step/
q: Put a stop to the incessant praising and rewarding. You see, in an effort to “catch them doing something good,” difficult students are often showered with praise and rewards and high fives for merely doing what they’re supposed to do.
It tells them loud and clear that they can’t do it, that they’re different from the other students, that they don’t have the same capabilities.
By refusing to placate him with made-up certificates, throwaway lines of false praise, or ginned up enthusiasm, you’ll be giving him a precious gift: His first taste of dignity.
It means that when you do praise him, it will only be because it is well earned. It will only be because real change in behavior has taken place—proven under your skeptical, watchful eye.
A knowing look or nod from across the room, a carefully written note attached to the inside of his desk, a whisper in his ear . . .
So now what? First Things First. When an unusually difficult student winds up in your classroom, your first step is to do what none of his previous teachers have done before you.
x: The first step with an unusually difficult student is to stop the common practice of constantly praising them for merely expected behavior.
Excessive 'caught being good' praise unintentionally communicates that the student is different and incapable, damaging self-worth.

Treating the student as fully capable, without lowering the bar, gives them what he calls their 'first taste of dignity.' Genuine praise should still occur, but only for real, proven accomplishment, and delivered…
Genuine praise should still be given, but only for real, proven accomplishment under a teacher's skeptical, watchful eye.
Authentic praise should be delivered quietly and personally — a look, a note, a whisper — rather than as public fanfare.
